title: Man. Post. Cap. II: Placeus — his own argument; mediate looks to Adam's actual first sin
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. Does that argumentation, which is wholly mine, overturn my cause? Do I contend sharply that Adam's actual disobedience itself is imputed to none of the posterity, that no one bears its penalties, that no one can be held guilty for it? What is clearer than that I rather contend it is imputed to Adam's posterity, that they bear its penalties, that they are held guilty for it? Otherwise, to what end did I set hereditary corruption apart from the state of the question? Why did I bring the distinction of immediate and mediate imputation? Why did I judge the attribute of the question to be thus distinguished: Whether Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to us as we are born? Why, when constituting the state of the controversy, did I apply to it a limitation sought from that distinction? To what end also do those very reasons pertain which I had proposed jointly and the Learned Man disjoined? I certainly wanted to give a reason why some sin is imputed to us, did I not? My words are too clear for that to be denied. What sin then did I mean? I could mean none but Adam's first actual. I said hereditary corruption is the habit which the first sin left in Adam's soul: do you not see I can understand no other first sin than that first actual? I said that corruption is a propensity to like sins, namely like that first actual; others cannot be understood. I said it is habitual consent to that sin. Who does not see that by that sin I do not mean the corruption, but that first actual by which Adam himself corrupted himself?
pass_b_english: Placeus: Is my own argument suddenly against me? Am I the one insisting that Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to none of his posterity, that nobody bears its penalties, that nobody can be held guilty for it? The opposite is clearer: I insist that it is imputed to Adam's posterity, that they bear its penalties, that they are held guilty for it. If not, why peel hereditary corruption out of the state of the question? Why introduce immediate versus mediate imputation? Why frame the question's attribute as Whether Adam's actual disobedience is imputed to us as we are born? Why, when I fixed the controversy's state, attach a limit drawn from that distinction? And why do the reasons I had set out together—and the Learned Man tore apart—matter at all? I was giving a reason why some sin is imputed to us. The wording is too open to allow denial. Which sin? Only Adam's first actual. When I called hereditary corruption the habit the first sin left in Adam's soul, I could not mean any other first sin than that first actual. When I called it a bent toward like sins, I meant like that first actual—nothing else fits. When I called it habitual consent to that sin, I meant by that sin not the corruption itself, but the first actual act by which Adam corrupted himself.
source_text: PLAC. Itane argumentatio, quae tota mea est, causam meam evertit? Itane contendo acriter ipsam Adami actualem inobedientiam nemini posterorum imputari, neminem ejus poenas ferre, neminem propter eam reum haberi posse? Quid clarius, quam me potius contendere eam Adami posteris imputari, eos ejus poenas ferre, propter eam reos haberi? Alioqui, quorsum seposui corruptionem haereditariam a statu quaestionis? Cur imputationis immediatae & mediatae distinctionem attuli? Cur sic distinguendum censui attributum quaestionis, Utrum actualis inobedientia Adami nobis nascentibus imputetur? Cur constituens statum controversiae ei limitationem ab illa distinctione petitam adhibui? Quorsum etiam pertinent istae ipsae rationes, quas conjunctim proposueram & Vir Doctus disjunxit? Volui certe rationem reddere, cur peccatum aliquod nobis imputetur, nonne? Nimis diserta sunt verba mea quam ut id possit negari. Quod ergo peccatum intellexi? Nullum potui, praeter actuale primum Adami. Dixi corruptionem haereditariam esse habitum, quem primum peccatum reliquit in Adami anima: nonne vides me aliud primum peccatum intelligere non posse, quam actuale illud primum? Dixi illam corruptionem esse propensionem ad similia peccata, nempe similia illi primo actuali, alia intelligi non possunt. Dixi eam esse consensum habitualem ad illud peccatum. Quis non videt per illud peccatum me corruptionem non intelligere, sed actuale illud primum quo se ipse Adamus corrupit?
